[2025 summer phd math-stat — problem 4]

Part IV. Observe i.i.d. $(X_i, Y_i)$ with $\mathbb{E}(Y \mid X) = X^T\beta^*$; split $X = (Z, W^T)^T$, $\beta^* = (\theta^*, \alpha^{*T})^T$ with $Z, \theta^*$ scalar and $Z$ binary. Let $\hat\beta$ be the Lasso-penalized least squares estimator, and $\hat\gamma$ the Lasso-penalized logistic-regression estimator of $Z$ on $W$. Consider the debiased estimator $\tilde\theta = \frac{(Z - \mathrm{expit}(W\hat\gamma))^T(Y - W\hat\alpha)/n}{(Z - \mathrm{expit}(W\hat\gamma))^T Z/n}$, with $\mathrm{expit}(u) = e^u/(1 + e^u)$. The goal is the asymptotic expansion $\tilde\theta - \theta^* = \frac{(Z - \mathrm{expit}(W\bar\gamma))^T(Y - Z\theta^* - W\alpha^*)/n}{(Z - \mathrm{expit}(W\bar\gamma))^T Z/n} + o_p(n^{-1/2})$, reducing to establishing equation (4) in the exam.
1) Show $|(Z - \mathrm{expit}(W\hat\gamma))^T(Y - Z\theta^* - W\hat\alpha)/n - (Z - \mathrm{expit}(W\bar\gamma))^T(Y - Z\theta^* - W\alpha^*)/n| \le \underbrace{|(Z - \mathrm{expit}(W\hat\gamma))^T W(\hat\alpha - \alpha^*)/n|}_{I} + \underbrace{|(\mathrm{expit}(W\hat\gamma) - \mathrm{expit}(W\bar\gamma))^T(Y - Z\theta^* - W\alpha^*)/n|}_{II}$.
2) Show, under suitable conditions, $I = O_p(1)(|S_{\beta^*}| + |S_{\bar\gamma}|)\frac{\log(n\vee p)}{n}$. State the conditions explicitly (you may use standard $\hat\beta, \hat\gamma$ rate properties).
3) Show that for any $u, \tilde u \in \mathbb{R}$: $|\mathrm{expit}_2(u) - \mathrm{expit}_2(\tilde u)| \le \mathrm{expit}_2(\tilde u)|u - \tilde u|$ and $|\mathrm{expit}(u) - \mathrm{expit}(\tilde u) - \mathrm{expit}_2(\tilde u)(u - \tilde u)| \le \mathrm{expit}_2(\tilde u)(u - \tilde u)^2$, where $\mathrm{expit}_2(u) = \mathrm{expit}(u)(1 - \mathrm{expit}(u))$.

Let  
\[
\varepsilon_i:=Y_i-Z_i\theta^*-W_i^T\alpha^*,\qquad 
\pi(u):=\operatorname{expit}(u),\qquad 
q(u):=\operatorname{expit}_2(u)=\pi(u)\{1-\pi(u)\}.
\]
Write \(\pi_{\hat\gamma,i}:=\pi(W_i^T\hat\gamma)\), \(\pi_{\bar\gamma,i}:=\pi(W_i^T\bar\gamma)\), and \(q_{\bar\gamma,i}:=q(W_i^T\bar\gamma)\). Also put
\[
s_\beta:=|S_{\beta^*}|,\qquad s_\gamma:=|S_{\bar\gamma}|,\qquad L_n:=\log(n\vee p).
\]

I will use \(P_n f:=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\).

---

## 1) Algebraic decomposition

We need to bound
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\left|
\frac{(Z-\pi(W\hat\gamma))^T(Y-Z\theta^*-W\hat\alpha)}{n}
-
\frac{(Z-\pi(W\bar\gamma))^T(Y-Z\theta^*-W\alpha^*)}{n}
\right|.
\end{aligned}
\]

Since
\[
Y-Z\theta^*-W\hat\alpha
=
Y-Z\theta^*-W\alpha^* - W(\hat\alpha-\alpha^*)
=
\varepsilon-W(\hat\alpha-\alpha^*),
\]
we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{(Z-\pi(W\hat\gamma))^T(Y-Z\theta^*-W\hat\alpha)}{n}
-
\frac{(Z-\pi(W\bar\gamma))^T(Y-Z\theta^*-W\alpha^*)}{n} \\
&=
\frac{(Z-\pi(W\hat\gamma))^T(\varepsilon-W(\hat\alpha-\alpha^*))}{n}
-
\frac{(Z-\pi(W\bar\gamma))^T\varepsilon}{n} \\
&=
-\frac{(Z-\pi(W\hat\gamma))^T W(\hat\alpha-\alpha^*)}{n}
+
\frac{(\pi(W\bar\gamma)-\pi(W\hat\gamma))^T\varepsilon}{n}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, by the triangle inequality,
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\left|
\frac{(Z-\pi(W\hat\gamma))^T(Y-Z\theta^*-W\hat\alpha)}{n}
-
\frac{(Z-\pi(W\bar\gamma))^T(Y-Z\theta^*-W\alpha^*)}{n}
\right| \\
&\le 
\underbrace{\left|
\frac{(Z-\pi(W\hat\gamma))^T W(\hat\alpha-\alpha^*)}{n}
\right|}_{I}
+
\underbrace{\left|
\frac{(\pi(W\hat\gamma)-\pi(W\bar\gamma))^T\varepsilon}{n}
\right|}_{II}.
\end{aligned}
\]

That proves the desired inequality.

---

## 2) Bound for \(I\)

Assume the following standard high-dimensional Lasso conditions.

### Conditions for part 2

Let \(\lambda_\beta,\lambda_\gamma\asymp \sqrt{L_n/n}\).

1. The linear Lasso \(\hat\beta\) satisfies the usual oracle \(\ell_1\)-rate
   \[
   \|\hat\beta-\beta^*\|_1=O_p(s_\beta\lambda_\beta),
   \]
   which follows, for example, under the usual score condition
   \[
   \left\|\frac{X^T\varepsilon}{n}\right\|_\infty=O_p(\lambda_\beta)
   \]
   and a restricted eigenvalue/compatibility condition on the design \(X\) over \(S_{\beta^*}\).

2. The logistic Lasso estimator \(\hat\gamma\) is defined by
   \[
   \hat\gamma\in \arg\min_\gamma 
   \left\{
   \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\left[\log\{1+\exp(W_i^T\gamma)\}-Z_iW_i^T\gamma\right]
   +\lambda_\gamma\|\gamma\|_1
   \right\}.
   \]

Then the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions for the logistic Lasso give
\[
\left\|
\frac{W^T(Z-\pi(W\hat\gamma))}{n}
\right\|_\infty
\le \lambda_\gamma.
\]

Now, by Hölder’s inequality,
\[
\begin{aligned}
I
&=
\left|
(\hat\alpha-\alpha^*)^T
\frac{W^T(Z-\pi(W\hat\gamma))}{n}
\right| \\
&\le 
\|\hat\alpha-\alpha^*\|_1
\left\|
\frac{W^T(Z-\pi(W\hat\gamma))}{n}
\right\|_\infty \\
&\le 
\|\hat\beta-\beta^*\|_1 \lambda_\gamma.
\end{aligned}
\]
Using the Lasso \(\ell_1\)-rate,
\[
I
=
O_p(s_\beta\lambda_\beta\lambda_\gamma).
\]
Since \(\lambda_\beta\lambda_\gamma\asymp L_n/n\),
\[
I
=
O_p(1)\,s_\beta\frac{L_n}{n}.
\]
In particular,
\[
I
=
O_p(1)\,(s_\beta+s_\gamma)\frac{L_n}{n}.
\]

---

## 3) Logistic derivative inequalities

There is an important issue: the two inequalities as stated in the problem are not true globally for all \(u,\tilde u\in\mathbb R\).

Indeed, take \(u=0\), \(\tilde u=10\). Then
\[
q(0)=\frac14,\qquad q(10)\approx 4.54\times 10^{-5}.
\]
The claimed inequality
\[
|q(u)-q(\tilde u)|\le q(\tilde u)|u-\tilde u|
\]
would require
\[
0.24995\lesssim 10(4.54\times 10^{-5})\approx 4.54\times 10^{-4},
\]
which is false.

Similarly,
\[
\left|
\pi(0)-\pi(10)-q(10)(0-10)
\right|
\approx 0.4995,
\]
while
\[
q(10)(0-10)^2\approx 0.00454,
\]
so the second claimed inequality is also false.

What is true, and what is sufficient for the statistical bound in part 4, is the following standard logistic self-concordance bound. Since
\[
q'(u)=q(u)\{1-2\pi(u)\},
\]
we have
\[
\left|\frac{q'(u)}{q(u)}\right|\le 1.
\]
Hence, for \(d=u-\tilde u\),
\[
q(\tilde u+t)\le e^{|t|}q(\tilde u).
\]
Therefore
\[
|q(u)-q(\tilde u)|
\le q(\tilde u)\{e^{|d|}-1\}
\le e^{|d|}q(\tilde u)|d|.
\]
Also, using Taylor’s formula,
\[
\pi(u)-\pi(\tilde u)-q(\tilde u)(u-\tilde u)
=
\int_0^{d} \{q(\tilde u+t)-q(\tilde u)\}\,dt,
\]
so
\[
\left|
\pi(u)-\pi(\tilde u)-q(\tilde u)(u-\tilde u)
\right|
\le
q(\tilde u)\{e^{|d|}-1-|d|\}
\le
\frac12 e^{|d|}q(\tilde u)d^2.
\]

Thus, on any event where \(|u-\tilde u|\le M\), one has
\[
|q(u)-q(\tilde u)|\le C_M q(\tilde u)|u-\tilde u|,
\]
and
\[
\left|
\pi(u)-\pi(\tilde u)-q(\tilde u)(u-\tilde u)
\right|
\le C_M q(\tilde u)(u-\tilde u)^2,
\]
for a constant \(C_M<\infty\). These corrected inequalities are what is needed below.

---

## 4) Bound for \(II\)

Recall
\[
II
=
\left|
\frac{(\pi(W\hat\gamma)-\pi(W\bar\gamma))^T\varepsilon}{n}
\right|.
\]

Assume additionally:

1. \(|\varepsilon_i|\le B_0\) a.s.

2. \(\bar\gamma\) is sparse with support \(S_{\bar\gamma}\), \(|S_{\bar\gamma}|=s_\gamma\).

3. The logistic Lasso satisfies the standard rates
   \[
   \|\hat\gamma-\bar\gamma\|_1
   =
   O_p(s_\gamma\lambda_\gamma),
   \]
   and
   \[
   \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
   q(W_i^T\bar\gamma)\{W_i^T(\hat\gamma-\bar\gamma)\}^2
   =
   O_p(s_\gamma\lambda_\gamma^2).
   \]
   These follow under the usual logistic score concentration and a weighted compatibility/restricted eigenvalue condition.

4. The empirical process term satisfies
   \[
   \left\|
   \frac1n W^T D_{\bar\gamma}\varepsilon
   \right\|_\infty
   =
   O_p(\lambda_\gamma),
   \]
   where
   \[
   D_{\bar\gamma}
   :=
   \operatorname{diag}\big(q(W_1^T\bar\gamma),\dots,q(W_n^T\bar\gamma)\big).
   \]
   This follows, for example, if the coordinates of \(W_i\) are uniformly bounded and \(\varepsilon_i\) is bounded, by Bernstein’s inequality and a union bound, because
   \[
   \mathbb E\!\left[W_{ij}q(W_i^T\bar\gamma)\varepsilon_i\right]=0
   \]
   since \(\mathbb E(\varepsilon_i\mid Z_i,W_i)=0\).

5. We have
   \[
   \max_{1\le i\le n}|W_i^T(\hat\gamma-\bar\gamma)|=O_p(1).
   \]
   A sufficient condition is uniformly bounded covariates \(\max_{i,j}|W_{ij}|\le C\) and \(s_\gamma\lambda_\gamma=O(1)\).

Let
\[
\delta_\gamma:=\hat\gamma-\bar\gamma,
\qquad
\eta_i:=W_i^T\delta_\gamma.
\]
By the corrected Taylor expansion from part 3,
\[
\pi(W_i^T\hat\gamma)-\pi(W_i^T\bar\gamma)
=
q(W_i^T\bar\gamma)\eta_i+r_i,
\]
with
\[
|r_i|
\le
C_n q(W_i^T\bar\gamma)\eta_i^2,
\qquad
C_n:=\frac12\exp\left(\max_i|\eta_i|\right)=O_p(1).
\]

Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
II
&=
\left|
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\varepsilon_i
\{\pi(W_i^T\hat\gamma)-\pi(W_i^T\bar\gamma)\}
\right| \\
&\le
\left|
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\varepsilon_i q(W_i^T\bar\gamma)W_i^T\delta_\gamma
\right|
+
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n|\varepsilon_i||r_i| \\
&\le
\left|
\delta_\gamma^T
\frac1n W^T D_{\bar\gamma}\varepsilon
\right|
+
B_0 C_n
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
q(W_i^T\bar\gamma)\eta_i^2.
\end{aligned}
\]

For the first term, Hölder’s inequality gives
\[
\left|
\delta_\gamma^T
\frac1n W^T D_{\bar\gamma}\varepsilon
\right|
\le
\|\delta_\gamma\|_1
\left\|
\frac1n W^T D_{\bar\gamma}\varepsilon
\right\|_\infty.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\left|
\delta_\gamma^T
\frac1n W^T D_{\bar\gamma}\varepsilon
\right|
=
O_p(s_\gamma\lambda_\gamma)\,O_p(\lambda_\gamma)
=
O_p(s_\gamma\lambda_\gamma^2).
\]

For the remainder term,
\[
B_0 C_n
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
q(W_i^T\bar\gamma)\eta_i^2
=
O_p(1)\,O_p(s_\gamma\lambda_\gamma^2)
=
O_p(s_\gamma\lambda_\gamma^2).
\]

Thus
\[
II
=
O_p(s_\gamma\lambda_\gamma^2).
\]
Since \(\lambda_\gamma^2\asymp L_n/n\),
\[
II
=
O_p(1)\,s_\gamma\frac{L_n}{n}.
\]
In particular,
\[
II
=
O_p(1)\,(s_\beta+s_\gamma)\frac{L_n}{n}.
\]

---

## Conclusion

From parts 1, 2, and 4,
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\left|
\frac{(Z-\pi(W\hat\gamma))^T(Y-Z\theta^*-W\hat\alpha)}{n}
-
\frac{(Z-\pi(W\bar\gamma))^T(Y-Z\theta^*-W\alpha^*)}{n}
\right| \\
&\qquad\le I+II \\
&\qquad=
O_p(1)(s_\beta+s_\gamma)\frac{\log(n\vee p)}{n}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, if
\[
(s_\beta+s_\gamma)\frac{\log(n\vee p)}{\sqrt n}=o(1),
\]
then
\[
\left|
\frac{(Z-\pi(W\hat\gamma))^T(Y-Z\theta^*-W\hat\alpha)}{n}
-
\frac{(Z-\pi(W\bar\gamma))^T(Y-Z\theta^*-W\alpha^*)}{n}
\right|
=
o_p(n^{-1/2}),
\]
which is the desired equation \((4)\)-type bound.

\[
\left|\frac{q'(u)}{q(u)}\right|\le 1.
\]
Hence, for \(d=u-\tilde u\),
\[
q(\tilde u+t)\le e^{|t|}q(\tilde u).
\]
Therefore
\[
|q(u)-q(\tilde u)|
\le q(\tilde u)\{e^{|d|}-1\}
\le e^{|d|}q(\tilde u)|d|.
\]
Also, using Taylor’s formula,
\[
\pi(u)-\pi(\tilde u)-q(\tilde u)(u-\tilde u)
=
\int_0^{d} \{q(\tilde u+t)-q(\tilde u)\}\,dt,
\]
so
\[
\left|
\pi(u)-\pi(\tilde u)-q(\tilde u)(u-\tilde u)
\right|
\le
q(\tilde u)\{e^{|d|}-1-|d|\}
\le
\frac12 e^{|d|}q(\tilde u)d^2.
\]

Thus, on any event where \(|u-\tilde u|\le M\), one has
\[
|q(u)-q(\tilde u)|\le C_M q(\tilde u)|u-\tilde u|,
\]
and
\[
\left|
\pi(u)-\pi(\tilde u)-q(\tilde u)(u-\tilde u)
\right|
\le C_M q(\tilde u)(u-\tilde u)^2,
\]
for a constant \(C_M<\infty\). These corrected inequalities are what is needed below.

---

## 4) Bound for \(II\)

Recall
\[
II
=
\left|
\frac{(\pi(W\hat\gamma)-\pi(W\bar\gamma))^T\varepsilon}{n}
\right|.
\]

Assume additionally:

1. \(|\varepsilon_i|\le B_0\) a.s.

2. \(\bar\gamma\) is sparse with support \(S_{\bar\gamma}\), \(|S_{\bar\gamma}|=s_\gamma\).

3. The logistic Lasso satisfies the standard rates
   \[
   \|\hat\gamma-\bar\gamma\|_1
   =
   O_p(s_\gamma\lambda_\gamma),
   \]
   and
   \[
   \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
   q(W_i^T\bar\gamma)\{W_i^T(\hat\gamma-\bar\gamma)\}^2
   =
   O_p(s_\gamma\lambda_\gamma^2).
   \]
   These follow under the usual logistic score concentration and a weighted compatibility/restricted eigenvalue condition.

4. The empirical process term satisfies
   \[
   \left\|
   \frac1n W^T D_{\bar\gamma}\varepsilon
   \right\|_\infty
   =
   O_p(\lambda_\gamma),
   \]
   where
   \[
   D_{\bar\gamma}
   :=
   \operatorname{diag}\big(q(W_1^T\bar\gamma),\dots,q(W_n^T\bar\gamma)\big).
   \]
   This follows, for example, if the coordinates of \(W_i\) are uniformly bounded and \(\varepsilon_i\) is bounded, by Bernstein’s inequality and a union bound, because
   \[
   \mathbb E\!\left[W_{ij}q(W_i^T\bar\gamma)\varepsilon_i\right]=0
   \]
   since \(\mathbb E(\varepsilon_i\mid Z_i,W_i)=0\).

5. We have
   \[
   \max_{1\le i\le n}|W_i^T(\hat\gamma-\bar\gamma)|=O_p(1).
   \]
   A sufficient condition is uniformly bounded covariates \(\max_{i,j}|W_{ij}|\le C\) and \(s_\gamma\lambda_\gamma=O(1)\).

Let
\[
\delta_\gamma:=\hat\gamma-\bar\gamma,
\qquad
\eta_i:=W_i^T\delta_\gamma.
\]
By the corrected Taylor expansion from part 3,
\[
\pi(W_i^T\hat\gamma)-\pi(W_i^T\bar\gamma)
=
q(W_i^T\bar\gamma)\eta_i+r_i,
\]
with
\[
|r_i|
\le
C_n q(W_i^T\bar\gamma)\eta_i^2,
\qquad
C_n:=\frac12\exp\left(\max_i|\eta_i|\right)=O_p(1).
\]

Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
II
&=
\left|
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\varepsilon_i
\{\pi(W_i^T\hat\gamma)-\pi(W_i^T\bar\gamma)\}
\right| \\
&\le
\left|
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\varepsilon_i q(W_i^T\bar\gamma)W_i^T\delta_\gamma
\right|
+
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n|\varepsilon_i||r_i| \\
&\le
\left|
\delta_\gamma^T
\frac1n W^T D_{\bar\gamma}\varepsilon
\right|
+
B_0 C_n
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
q(W_i^T\bar\gamma)\eta_i^2.
\end{aligned}
\]

For the first term, Hölder’s inequality gives
\[
\left|
\delta_\gamma^T
\frac1n W^T D_{\bar\gamma}\varepsilon
\right|
\le
\|\delta_\gamma\|_1
\left\|
\frac1n W^T D_{\bar\gamma}\varepsilon
\right\|_\infty.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\left|
\delta_\gamma^T
\frac1n W^T D_{\bar\gamma}\varepsilon
\right|
=
O_p(s_\gamma\lambda_\gamma)\,O_p(\lambda_\gamma)
=
O_p(s_\gamma\lambda_\gamma^2).
\]

For the remainder term,
\[
B_0 C_n
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
q(W_i^T\bar\gamma)\eta_i^2
=
O_p(1)\,O_p(s_\gamma\lambda_\gamma^2)
=
O_p(s_\gamma\lambda_\gamma^2).
\]

Thus
\[
II
=
O_p(s_\gamma\lambda_\gamma^2).
\]
Since \(\lambda_\gamma^2\asymp L_n/n\),
\[
II
=
O_p(1)\,s_\gamma\frac{L_n}{n}.
\]
In particular,
\[
II
=
O_p(1)\,(s_\beta+s_\gamma)\frac{L_n}{n}.
\]

---

## Conclusion

From parts 1, 2, and 4,
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\left|
\frac{(Z-\pi(W\hat\gamma))^T(Y-Z\theta^*-W\hat\alpha)}{n}
-
\frac{(Z-\pi(W\bar\gamma))^T(Y-Z\theta^*-W\alpha^*)}{n}
\right| \\
&\qquad\le I+II \\
&\qquad=
O_p(1)(s_\beta+s_\gamma)\frac{\log(n\vee p)}{n}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, if
\[
(s_\beta+s_\gamma)\frac{\log(n\vee p)}{\sqrt n}=o(1),
\]
then
\[
\left|
\frac{(Z-\pi(W\hat\gamma))^T(Y-Z\theta^*-W\hat\alpha)}{n}
-
\frac{(Z-\pi(W\bar\gamma))^T(Y-Z\theta^*-W\alpha^*)}{n}
\right|
=
o_p(n^{-1/2}),
\]
which is the desired equation \((4)\)-type bound.
